newsitem.title: NORWAY: FOCUS-Statoil thrives on high oil prices.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Statoil thrives on high oil prices.

text.p: Norway's state-owned energy company Statoil said on Thursday operating profits in the first half of 1997 jumped 23 percent to 10.1 billion crowns ($1.3 billion) primarily because of higher oil prices.
In the year-ago period Statoil, or Den norske stats oljeselskap AS, booked operating profits of 8.2 billion crowns.
Six-month net profits rose 12.5 percent to 2.7 billion crowns compared with 2.4 billion crowns, while overall revenues amounted to 59.1 billion crowns versus 49.5 billion crowns.

However, a rise in the dollar/crown exchange rate yielded an unrealised currency loss on the group's debt, and net financial costs increased fivefold to 2.5 billion crowns in the first half from 500 million.

Statoil is responsible for roughly half of Norway's 3.2 million barrel per day (bpd) of oil production and markets around two million bpd -- comprising own equity and the state's share. This puts Statoil among the world's top three crude sellers alongside Saudi Aramco and the National Iranian Oil Co.
The Stavanger-based group said it saw no major changes in any of its markets, although oil prices were expected to soften in the second half.
"We do not see anything on the horizon that should change the pattern (in markets) we observe now," John Ove Lindoe, Statoil's chief spokesman, told Reuters.
"The trend in oil prices is a little downwards and we estimate that the second half of 1997 will show lower prices. So we expect results in the second half to be slightly below the first."

Statoil said exploration and production achieved a first-half operating profit of 9.5 billion crowns, against 7.6 billion crowns, although equity oil supply slipped to an average 445,000 bpd compared with 453,000 bpd.
"The slight decline in equity crude production was expected and we are working on our goal to maintain net equity production on the Norwegian continental shelf at 500,000 bpd," Lindoe said.
He said that the start-up of the 160,000 bpd Norne oilfield would go to plan sometime in August.
Gas sales in the six months rose to a total 19.2 billion cubic metres against 18.5 billion cubic metres.

Operating profits from refining and marketing dropped 36 percent to 571 million crowns versus 896 million crowns between January and June in 1996 because of a squeeze on margins in retail sales in Scandinavia due to price competition.
The group also agreed in June the sale of its German service station network to Shell.
It said refinery operations yielded stronger results on the back of increased margins, high regularity and improvements in cost efficiency.

The company's shipping arm, which will be spun off in the autumn to form a new separate company with Norway's Rasmussen group, also showed an improved performance due to higher freight rates and good utilisation of the fleet.
Statoil said petrochemicals moved into the black with first-half operating profits of 162 million crowns compared with a 19 million crown loss a year ago.
Statoil is 50 percent owner of the Borealis petrochemicals group with Finland's Neste Oy.

"We have a rather firm belief in the petrochemicals markets, although they are almost impossible to predict," Lindoe said, adding that Statoil was satisfied with current methanol prices of around 330 to 340 marks per tonne.
The company started up in June methanol production at the 800,000 tonne per year Tjeldbergodden plant in mid-Norway.
"We note with satisfaction that our production at Tjeldbergodden has entered the market at not an 'unfriendly' price regime for us," Lindoe said.
--Oslo newsroom, +47 22 42 50 41 ($ = 7.485 Norwegian Crowns)
